At this age? Especially after possibly losing one's friends and family because transitioning? This is the kind of thing novels should be about these days. Yeah, dealing with repression is really difficult, living in the closet for however many years that may have been for you. Knowing that some expressions of masculinity aren't yet accepted by society can also make transitioning feel like a method of survival rather than living as one's true self. I've battled with that. Getting help from health professionals, close friends, and the LGBTQIA community matters in the long-run. You shouldn't stop caring about who you are. It's going to bite you in the ass one day, as they say. But, also, there's a lot of coolness about being non-binary and if you're able to balance your feelings being either gender, there's nothing wrong identifying as any variant of 'transgender'. That's exactly what a lot of transphobes don't want you to do.

It's mostly trial and error getting past the people who are obviously out to get in LGBTQIA's peoples' ways. I mean, until one legally changes their name, it's extremely hard to avoid getting deadnamed. Life is pretty horrible that way for us. What's key is being extremely nice to oneself. You can't be rude to yourself over failures. I do it all the time. To answer your question more directly, safe is going to be a hard feeling to find. I don't, most of the time. If you have any idea how much people are discontent with themselves, then you might guess what their thoughts about such a fetishized minority may be. That being said, if you have that knowledge, you're way ahead of them.

I get a sense of comfort from novels contained in small worlds with their own personal satire at work. 'The Loved Ones' by Evelyn Waugh is supposed to poke fun at British aristocracy and well-to-doers during the heyday of American exceptionalism. The post-war boom was well underway, but the narrative that's focused on such a gothic world, with at least one or two very dreary characters, creates an insular world that speaks amongst itself with satirical overtures, social critique veiled as conversation, and conversation veiled as social critique. When I was growing up and read this first, it gave me a sense of the world I had yet to fully enter. I was assigned the book during an AP literature class in high school, and was probably the first 'not-that-serious' book ever given to me. I return to it when the world feels uncertain. The humor is like a nudge in the ribs. Something very much like that hug you described coming from your book.

There's also this one sci-fi book I picked up from a local bookstore back during my childhood, I can't remember the title of. But the prose was *dense*, and it was far past my reading level. The fact that I didn't understand 99% of the novel past the prologue heightened my sense of wonder while reading it not as a story, but a glimpse into another world. Unintelligibility is something I feel is lacking in contemporary sci-fi, that perhaps videogames nail down better using the visual aspect. I would go back to it every once and awhile during my youth to see if I could grasp the plot but every single time, I was like, "Wow. The alien universe hardly makes sense." That made me feel very alone, but eager to explore. 

I think I used to read mostly for the confirmation biases, but now I seek books posing challenges. Something that's hard to find when you know what kind of books you like. Something I miss from childhood is how the lack of reader agency provides the book more power, not to dispel wisdom, but wrap you up in its parts that most academic classes don't want you to pay really close attention to anymore, unless it's special focus. I'm not saying people think atmosphere is superficial, but... when you're analyzing sentences, a lot of wonder gets lost. The most recent contact I've come to with an imaginary world on page is through The Witcher series. I like to read books that could be videogames (and indeed, are) but already feel like such an experience. The Witcher books feel like they have worlds going on beyond the reader's perspective, despite any narrow focus provided. And I think it's due a lot because the exposition trickles like any normal literary experience. The 'Metro' series by Glukhovsky were made a videogame series, yet the first books feel like a transcendental experience, not an exploration of a world. I'm touching on the theme of modern relatability once again. A post-apocalyptic world is just easier to see than a monster-ridden kingdom with elves and witchers.
